prompt: On a binary A-B hull, A is at (0, 0), AB at (0.5, -1.0 eV/atom) and B at (1, 0). A new compound A3B (fraction of B 0.25) has a formation energy of -0.40 eV/atom, and no other phases exist. What does the hull say?

options.text: It is 0.10 eV/atom above the hull and decomposes into A and AB
options.why: The hull at x = 0.25 lies halfway along the segment from A to AB, at -0.50 eV/atom. The compound sits 0.10 eV/atom higher, so splitting into A and AB (A3B to 2A + AB) lowers the energy.

options.text: It is stable because its formation energy is negative
options.why: Tempting, but negative only means lower than the elements. The test is against every mixture of other phases, and A plus AB is lower here.

options.text: It is 0.40 eV/atom above the hull
options.why: That compares it with the elements at zero. The hull at this composition is set by A and AB, not by the elements alone.

options.text: It decomposes into AB and B
options.why: B lies on the other side of AB. A composition of 0.25 sits between A (0) and AB (0.5), so those are the products.

prompt: You want to put a transition-metal oxide computed with GGA+U on the same hull as the metal computed with plain GGA. What does the Materials Project scheme do?

options.text: It computes each with its own method and adds a fitted energy per transition-metal atom to the GGA+U compound
options.why: Jain and co-workers fitted these corrections so that GGA and GGA+U energies share one hull; MP2020 refitted them with uncertainties.

options.text: It subtracts the two energies directly; U cancels out
options.why: U adds an energy term that depends on the d occupation, which differs between metal and oxide. It does not cancel.

options.text: It recomputes the metal with the same U, so no correction is needed
options.why: A U on a metal spoils its description; the scheme avoids that by keeping the metal at GGA and correcting the oxide.

options.text: It ignores the oxides and builds the hull from metals only
options.why: Then no oxide could be judged at all. The correction exists precisely to mix the two classes.

prompt: A screening study keeps every candidate within 25 meV/atom of the hull. Which description of that cut-off is honest?

options.text: A heuristic, about the thermal energy at room temperature; many known compounds are metastable and some sit further above
options.why: k_B T at 300 K is about 25.9 meV, and surveys of known crystals find a spread of metastability. The number is a rule of thumb, not a law.

options.text: A law: compounds above 25 meV/atom cannot be made
options.why: Tempting because a threshold looks sharp, but many synthesized materials lie above such cut-offs; kinetics can trap them.

options.text: It guarantees that every compound below it can be made
options.why: The hull ignores kinetics, entropy and missing competing phases, so passing the filter guarantees nothing.

options.text: It is the error bar of PBE energies
options.why: It is not an error estimate; it is a screening choice tied loosely to the thermal energy.

prompt: Your new ternary oxide comes out on the hull, but you left out one known competing ternary phase. What is the risk?

options.text: The hull is drawn too high, so the compound can look stable when it is not
options.why: A missing phase can only remove points from below; with it included, the hull could pass below your compound and give it a positive energy above the hull.

options.text: None: the hull only uses binary phases
options.why: A ternary hull uses every phase in the chemical system, ternaries included.

options.text: The compound will look less stable than it is
options.why: Adding phases can only lower the hull, so leaving one out can only flatter the compound.

options.text: The formation energy per atom changes
options.why: The formation energy depends only on the compound and the elemental references; the hull is what changes.

prompt: In the nudged elastic band, which parts of the forces act on each image?

options.text: The true force perpendicular to the path and the spring force along it
options.why: The perpendicular true force pulls the band onto the valley floor; the parallel spring force keeps the images spaced. This projection is the nudge.

options.text: The full true force and the full spring force
options.why: Then the images slide down into the end valleys and the springs cut corners: the band drifts off the minimum energy path.

options.text: The true force along the path and the spring force perpendicular to it
options.why: That is reversed: the true force along the path would push images into the minima.

options.text: Only the spring force
options.why: Without the true force the band never finds the valley floor; it stays a straight line.

hints: Which force should push the band onto the valley floor?
Which force should keep the images apart?

items.label: Compute the true force on each image

visual.alt: A four-step flow: compute the force on each image, project with the path tangent, add spring forces, move the images.

prompt: Why turn on the climbing image (LCLIMB = .TRUE.) for the final NEB run?

options.text: So that the highest image ends exactly on the saddle point and the barrier is not underestimated
options.why: The climbing image drops its springs and has the force along the path reversed, so it climbs to the saddle; plain images only bracket it.

options.text: To make the springs stiffer
options.why: The climbing image removes the springs on one image; it does not change the spring constant of the others.

options.text: To relax the two end points
options.why: The end points stay fixed in NEB; they must be relaxed beforehand.

options.text: To find a second, lower path
options.why: It refines the same path; finding a different path needs a different starting guess.

hints: Does any plain image sit exactly on the highest point?
What happens to the climbing image's force along the path?

visual.alt: A three-step flow: converge a plain elastic band, restart with the climbing image switched on, read the barrier.

prompt: You run a CI-NEB with 5 images and the VTST optimizer. Which setup is right?

options.text: Folders 00 to 06, IMAGES = 5, IBRION = 3 and POTIM = 0, a rank count divisible by 5
options.why: 00 and 06 hold the end points, 01 to 05 the images; IBRION = 3 with POTIM = 0 hands the moves to the VTST optimizer, and each image gets an equal share of ranks.

options.text: Folders 01 to 05, IMAGES = 7
options.why: The end points need their own folders, 00 and N+1, and IMAGES counts only the movable images.

options.text: IBRION = 2 and POTIM = 0.5 with IOPT = 1
options.why: With IBRION = 2 VASP's own optimizer also moves the images; the VTST optimizers expect IBRION = 3 and POTIM = 0.

options.text: Any number of MPI ranks
options.why: The ranks are split evenly over the images, so the count must be a multiple of IMAGES.

hints: How many folders hold the end points?
Which VASP optimizer setting leaves the moves to VTST?

visual.caption: Preparing an NEB run.
visual.alt: A four-step flow: relax the end points, create the numbered folders, set the image count and the optimizer, run.

prompt: A frequency calculation on your converged climbing image shows two imaginary modes. What does that mean?

options.text: It is a higher-order saddle, not a transition state; rethink the path
options.why: A first-order saddle has exactly one imaginary mode, along the path. Two mean the structure is a maximum in a second direction too.

options.text: It is a confirmed transition state
options.why: A transition state has exactly one imaginary mode; two is one too many.

options.text: It is a local minimum
options.why: A minimum has no imaginary modes at all.

options.text: Nothing; NEB results never need checking
options.why: An NEB that converged is a path, not a proof; the frequency check is what confirms the saddle.

hints: How many imaginary modes does a first-order saddle have?
What does an extra imaginary mode say about another direction?

items.label: Frequency run on the climbing image

visual.caption: Checking a saddle point.
visual.alt: A three-step flow: converge the climbing-image NEB, run a frequency calculation on the top image, count the imaginary modes.

prompt: Why does an AIMD run of a hydrogen-containing material need a smaller POTIM than one of a heavy-atom oxide?

options.text: Light atoms vibrate faster, so the time step must be shorter to follow them
options.why: A spring's frequency goes as one over the square root of the mass, so hydrogen vibrates fastest; the Field Handbook uses 0.5 fs with hydrogen instead of 1 fs.

options.text: Hydrogen needs a higher ENCUT
options.why: The cutoff is a separate convergence choice; the time step is about how fast the atoms move.

options.text: Hydrogen atoms are larger
options.why: Size is not the issue; mass is. Hydrogen is the lightest atom.

options.text: The thermostat does not work with hydrogen
options.why: Thermostats work with any atoms; the problem is resolving fast vibrations.

hints: How does the frequency of a spring depend on the mass?
What happens if a step is a large fraction of a vibration period?

visual.caption: Choosing an MD time step.
visual.alt: A three-step flow: choose a time step, run a short constant-energy test, check that the total energy stays constant.

prompt: In an NVE run the total energy drifts steadily upward. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The time step is too large or the electronic convergence too loose
options.why: In NVE the total energy is conserved by the equations of motion; drift means the integration or the forces are not accurate enough.

options.text: The thermostat is too weak
options.why: NVE has no thermostat; that is what makes the total energy a clean check.

options.text: Nothing; the total energy always rises in MD
options.why: In NVE it should fluctuate around a constant.

options.text: The cell is too small
options.why: A small cell gives noisy averages, but it does not make a conserved quantity drift.

hints: Which quantity is conserved in NVE?
What controls the accuracy of each step?

visual.caption: An energy conservation check.
visual.alt: A three-step flow: run a constant-energy simulation, plot the total energy against time, look for a drift.

prompt: In the straight, long-time part of an MSD curve from a 3D simulation, the MSD grows by 6.0 square angstrom every 10 ps. What is the diffusion coefficient, in square angstrom per ps?
hints: In three dimensions, D is the slope of the MSD divided by 6.
The slope is 6.0 / 10 square angstrom per ps.

visual.caption: From a trajectory to a diffusion coefficient.
visual.alt: A four-step flow: unwrap the coordinates, compute the mean squared displacement, fit its straight part, divide the slope by six.

prompt: Which MDALGO does VASP use for an NPT run, as pymatgen's NPT input set writes it?

options.text: MDALGO = 3 (Langevin) with ISIF = 3, LANGEVIN_GAMMA, LANGEVIN_GAMMA_L and PMASS
options.why: The Langevin thermostat with a lattice friction and a lattice mass lets the cell change; ISIF = 3 turns on the cell degrees of freedom.

options.text: MDALGO = 2 (Nose-Hoover) with ISIF = 0
options.why: ISIF = 0 does not even compute the stress, so the cell cannot respond to pressure.

options.text: IBRION = 2 with ISIF = 3
options.why: That is a relaxation of the cell, not molecular dynamics.

options.text: MDALGO = 1 with ANDERSEN_PROB = 0
options.why: That switches the Andersen thermostat off, giving constant energy, not constant pressure.

hints: Which thermostat does the pymatgen NPT set use?
Which ISIF lets the cell shape and volume change?

items.label: Set the cell degrees of freedom

visual.caption: Setting up an MD ensemble.
visual.alt: A three-step flow: pick the ensemble, pick the thermostat, set which cell degrees of freedom may change.

prompt: During on-the-fly MLFF training in VASP, when does VASP do a DFT calculation instead of using the force field?

options.text: When the Bayesian estimate of the force-field error is too large
options.why: The force field predicts forces and an error estimate at every step; a large estimate triggers a first-principles step, whose result joins the training set.

options.text: At every step, the force field is only used afterwards
options.why: Then training would cost as much as plain AIMD; skipping most DFT steps is the point of on-the-fly learning.

options.text: Never, the force field is trained on an empty set
options.why: Training needs DFT data; the first steps and the uncertain ones are computed with DFT.

options.text: Only at the last step
options.why: A single DFT step at the end could not train anything.

hints: What does a Bayesian fit give besides the prediction?
Why would you want DFT exactly where the model is unsure?

items.label: Predict forces and an error estimate
Error too large: run DFT and learn
Error small: move with the force field

visual.caption: One step of on-the-fly learning.
visual.alt: A three-step flow: the force field predicts forces with an error estimate, a large estimate triggers a DFT step, a small one lets the run move on.
